passage:
"Sir, do you have five minutes? It's about the survey data."
Professor Darshan looked up from his laptop. "Come in, Rukmini."
"Last night I was cleaning the response sheet and deleted forty rows by mistake. I saved before I noticed."
"Forty out of how many?"
"Two hundred and ten. I found an older copy from Monday on the shared drive, so only Tuesday's and Wednesday's responses are gone. That's the forty."
"Hmm. And what do you plan to do?"
"I've already written to the class reps who circulated the form, asking those students to fill it in again. I've also turned on version history so this can't happen silently again. The analysis may be two days late. I wanted you to hear it from me first, not in the report."
He took off his glasses. "Most people tell me after the deadline. Send me the new timeline tonight."
"I will. Thank you, Sir."
As she left, he was already writing a note for the other groups: turn on version history.

qa.q: How many rows did Rukmini delete?
qa.a: Forty rows, out of two hundred and ten.

qa.q: What does Professor Darshan's reply suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels respect, even some admiration, because most people tell him after the deadline and Rukmini came early with a plan.

qa.q: Which parts of Rukmini's message made it work?
qa.a: Rukmini said exactly what happened and how much was lost, what was already being done to recover and prevent it, and the likely delay, all before the deadline.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had waited until the report was due?
qa.a: The professor would hear it late, there would be less time to collect the responses again, and trust would likely drop.

grounding: Shows a young adult telling a professor about a mistake early, with what happened and what they will do about it.

passage:
Jyoti, you asked why I left the warehouse job. Here's the real reason. Our shift manager kept a whiteboard by the canteen, "Errors this week", with our names in red. Everyone read it at lunch. After my name went up once for a wrong pallet count, I, Hansa, stopped reporting anything. So did everyone else.
In March the label printer started skipping a digit on some pin codes. I noticed on Tuesday. I fixed my own parcels by hand and said nothing, because whoever reported it would "own" it. Turns out three of us had noticed. Nobody spoke.
By Friday about four hundred parcels had gone to the wrong sorting hub. The manager shouted for an hour and asked who knew. Silence again. I sat there knowing I could have stopped it on day one, and too scared to say so even then.

qa.q: What was written on the whiteboard by the canteen?
qa.a: "Errors this week", with the workers' names in red.

qa.q: Why did Hansa keep quiet about the label printer?
qa.a: Hansa was scared of being named and blamed, since whoever reported a problem would "own" it and end up on the red board.

qa.q: What could the manager have done instead of the red board?
qa.a: The manager could thank people for raising problems early and look at what in the process went wrong, so someone would speak up on day one.

qa.q: What would change if one of the three workers had felt safe to speak on Tuesday?
qa.a: The skipped digit could have been fixed on Tuesday, and about four hundred parcels would not have gone to the wrong hub.

grounding: Shows a worker in a team that punishes errors hiding a problem, which grows unseen because fear keeps everyone silent.

passage:
"Okay, Saturday's deliveries," Binita said, pen at the whiteboard. "Thirty families got nothing. Let's start with what happened, step by step."
Nilesh shifted in his chair. "I had the old route sheet. That's on me."
"Hold on. I'm not looking for who. Why was the old sheet in the van at all?"
"It was on the clipboard. The new one was only in the group chat."
Mariam added, "And that message came at midnight. Most drivers leave at seven without checking."
"So, the conditions," Binita said, writing. "Two versions of the route, one on paper, one on a phone. Nobody confirming which. What would stop it happening again?"
"One sheet only. The old one goes in the bin when the new one's printed," Nilesh said.
"And a quick call at seven where drivers read out their first stop," Mariam said.
Binita underlined both. "Good. Nilesh, will you print the sheets from now on? You've seen exactly where it breaks."
Nilesh nodded, his shoulders dropping.

qa.q: How many families got no delivery on Saturday?
qa.a: Thirty families got nothing.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he said "That's on me"?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty and braced for blame; his shoulders dropping at the end show relief once the focus moved to the system.

qa.q: What two changes did the team agree on?
qa.a: Keep one printed route sheet and bin the old one, and hold a quick seven o'clock call where drivers read out their first stop.

qa.q: What would change if Binita had accepted "That's on me" and moved on?
qa.a: The team would have blamed Nilesh and missed the real cause, two versions of the route and a midnight message, so it could happen again with another driver.

grounding: Shows a team reviewing a failure by asking what happened and what conditions allowed it, fixing the process instead of hunting a culprit.

subtype: Writing one lesson and one change [Response]
passage:
The seed distribution at the Rampur cooperative had been a mess. Farmers queued from seven, and by noon old Harbans ji was sitting in the dust, fanning himself with his cap. Uday, who ran the counter, spent the whole day looking up each name in a fat register.
That evening he sat on the cooperative's step with Divyansh, the secretary, and a cup of tea going cold. "I keep going over it," Uday said. "I should have hired more hands. Started earlier. Put up a tent..."
Divyansh stopped him. "That's a list of regrets. Give me one lesson and one change."
Uday thought. "Lesson: the register was the slow part, not the people. Change: next time I sort the names by village the week before, and each village gets its own hour."
Divyansh wrote it on the back of a receipt book and pinned it above the counter. "Now it's a plan."
In April the queue was gone by eleven.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh pin the note?
qa.a: Above the counter, written on the back of a receipt book.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling as he went over the day?
qa.a: Uday felt regretful and frustrated, listing everything he should have done while his tea went cold.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh ask for one lesson and one change?
qa.a: It turned Uday's long list of regrets into a single doable action, sorting names by village and giving each village its own hour.

qa.q: How might Harbans ji and the other farmers experience the April distribution?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved, with the queue gone by eleven instead of waiting in the dust till noon.

grounding: Shows a person ending a review with one lesson learned and one concrete change, rather than only regret.

subtype: Failing an exam and feeling finished [Actor]
passage:
Preeti, you're the only one I can say this to. When the board results came out, I saw "Fail" next to maths and my whole body went cold. Every other kid in my building passed. Sharma aunty had already sent sweets around for her son. Papa had told everyone at the shop I'd get science stream. I thought, that's it, Parul, you're finished. No science, no college, no job, everyone laughing.
I didn't eat. I lay facing the wall. Around ten, Mummy came and sat on my bed and didn't say a word about marks. She just held my hand and said, "We'll look at the compartment exam tomorrow, not tonight."
Today my tuition sir said lots of students clear it in July. I don't fully believe it yet. But it's been four days, and the world hasn't ended, even if it still feels a bit like it.

qa.q: What did Mummy say when she sat on the bed?
qa.a: "We'll look at the compartment exam tomorrow, not tonight."

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when the result came?
qa.a: Parul felt shocked and hopeless, body going cold, sure that one failed subject meant no science, no college and everyone laughing.

qa.q: What could help Parul in the days ahead?
qa.a: Taking one small step, like finding out about the July compartment exam with the tuition teacher, and keeping on talking to Mummy or Preeti when it feels heavy.

qa.q: Why might Mummy have avoided talking about marks that night?
qa.a: Mummy probably saw how hurt Parul was and chose comfort first, leaving the plans for the next day.

grounding: Shows a teenager who fails a major exam feeling the future has collapsed under family and neighbourhood expectations.

passage:
In Kumbakonam the results were pinned outside the school gate by nine. Karthik read his roll number twice, then walked home the long way, past the temple tank.
His father was waiting on the thinnai. "Trisha scored ninety-two. Your own cousin, same school, same teachers. What were you doing all year?"
His mother said nothing at all. She served dinner and cleared it in silence. The quiet was worse than the shouting.
For a week Karthik stayed in his room, skipped meals, and stopped answering his friends. On the eighth day he told his Periamma, "There's no point trying anything now."
Periamma sat down beside him right then. "You failed an exam. You didn't fail at being my boy." That afternoon she walked him to the school counsellor, Mrs Selvi, and waited outside. Walking home, she said, "We'll talk about the retest next week. Today, just eat with me."

qa.q: What did Karthik's father say Trisha scored?
qa.a: Trisha scored ninety-two.

qa.q: How did the comparison and the silence at home make Karthik feel?
qa.a: They left him more ashamed and hopeless, so he hid in his room, skipped meals and said there was no point trying.

qa.q: What did Periamma do that helped?
qa.a: Periamma comforted him first, said failing an exam was not failing as a person, took him to the counsellor that same afternoon, and left retest plans for later.

qa.q: What would change if Karthik's father had spoken to him the way Periamma did?
qa.a: Karthik might have felt supported instead of ashamed, and might not have shut himself away for a week.

grounding: Shows a student who failed meeting comparison and heavy silence at home, then support first and a counsellor's help.

subtype: Rejection from a placement or programme [Actor]
passage:
Honestly, Yogesh, I wasn't going to talk about this, but fine. You got the design internship. I didn't. I prepared for four months: portfolio redone twice, mock interviews every Sunday. When the list came out and my name wasn't on it, I smiled, said congratulations to you, and then went and sat in the bike shed for an hour.
I'm Jeevan, and I'll admit it: I was jealous. Not of you exactly; of that email. Then embarrassed, because everyone in our hostel knew I'd applied. Then worse: I started thinking maybe I'm just not good enough and my teachers were only being kind.
Yesterday the placement officer told me they took only two people from four hundred applications, and both had worked on packaging projects like theirs. My portfolio is all furniture. That helped a little. It still stings. I'm applying to a furniture studio in Jaipur next week.

qa.q: How many people did the internship take, and from how many applications?
qa.a: They took only two people from four hundred applications.

qa.q: What did Jeevan feel when the list came out?
qa.a: Jeevan felt jealous of the email, then embarrassed because the hostel knew, and then doubtful about being good enough at all.

qa.q: What next step is Jeevan taking, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Applying to a furniture studio next week fits, since Jeevan's portfolio is all furniture and the rejection was partly about fit.

qa.q: What might it be like for Yogesh to hear this?
qa.a: Yogesh might feel awkward and sad, learning that the smile and congratulations hid an hour alone in the bike shed.

grounding: Shows a young adult turned down after long preparation feeling envy, embarrassment and doubt, before seeing the role of fit and competition.

subtype: Rest, reframe, then a small next step [Response]
passage:
Ira, sit. You look the way I looked at twenty, after my first bakery stall failed at the college fest. I, your Kishore Mama, had baked two hundred rusks; I sold thirty. I carried the rest home on the bus and didn't touch the oven for three days. My mother let me be. She just kept putting tea next to me.
On the fourth day my friend Salim came over and made me take a sheet of paper. On one side, what I could control: the recipe, the price, where I stood. On the other, what I couldn't: it rained, and the fest moved indoors, away from my stall. Half my misery was on the second side.
Then he said, "One thing. Just one." So I baked twelve rusks, better ones, and sold them at the bus stand the next morning. All twelve. That was the start, beta. Not a big promise. Twelve rusks.

qa.q: How many rusks did Kishore bake for the fest, and how many sold?
qa.a: Kishore baked two hundred rusks and sold thirty.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling in the three days he didn't touch the oven?
qa.a: Kishore felt defeated and miserable after the failed stall, and needed time to feel bad before trying again.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around for Kishore?
qa.a: Sorting what he could control from what he couldn't, then baking just twelve better rusks and selling them the next morning, gave him a small win to build on.

qa.q: How did Kishore's mother handle his failure?
qa.a: She let him be and quietly kept putting tea next to him, giving comfort without pushing.

grounding: Shows a person letting themselves feel bad for a few days, separating what was and was not in their control, then taking one small step.

passage:
March 3. Avni pulled down the shutter of the tiffin kitchen for the last time. Eighteen months, forty regular customers at the peak, and now the lease was up and orders had dried to nine a day. She handed the keys to the landlord and walked straight past Dilnaz, who had come to help pack, because she couldn't trust her own voice.
March 20. Avni still hadn't opened her laptop. She told Dilnaz on the phone, "Maybe I'm just bad at judging things. Everyone said it was a risk." Dilnaz didn't argue. "You're allowed to be sad for a while. It was your baby."
April 14. At Dilnaz's dining table, Avni filled one page: what went wrong. Too far from the offices. Menu changed too often. Never asked customers why they stopped. At the bottom she wrote, "Next time: ask the people leaving." She read it twice. It felt less like a verdict and more like a map.

qa.q: How many orders a day was the kitchen getting at the end?
qa.a: Orders had dried to nine a day.

qa.q: Why did Avni walk straight past Dilnaz on March 3?
qa.a: Avni was grieving the kitchen and afraid of breaking down, because she couldn't trust her own voice.

qa.q: What did Avni's one page do well?
qa.a: It named concrete causes, the distance, a changing menu and never asking customers, and ended with one change for next time instead of blame.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz help Avni through those weeks?
qa.a: Dilnaz came to help pack, didn't argue with Avni's doubts, gave permission to be sad, and later offered a table to work through the lessons.

grounding: Shows a young professional grieving a failed venture, doubting their judgment, and later drawing concrete lessons.

subtype: Friend who is struggling after failure [Observer]
passage:
Last winter, after Darshan failed the civil services prelims for the third time, he went quiet. I, Binita, noticed it in small ways first: messages left on seen, his cricket kit gathering dust by my door where he'd dropped it, the lights off in his room when I walked past at seven.
I had a speech ready about many paths. I didn't give it. Instead I started turning up. I'd knock with two plates of rajma chawal and we'd eat and watch old matches. Some evenings he talked; most he didn't. Once I took his clothes to the laundry with mine. He said thanks as if it were a big thing.
After a month he was still sleeping till two and had skipped his cousin's wedding. So one night I said, gently, "I think talking to a counsellor might help. I'll sit with you while you book it, if you want." He was quiet a long time, then handed me his phone.

qa.q: What did Binita bring when knocking on Darshan's door?
qa.a: Two plates of rajma chawal.

qa.q: Why did Binita hold back the speech about many paths?
qa.a: Binita seems to have sensed Darshan was too hurt for a pep talk and cared more about simply being there, so Binita chose to keep turning up.

qa.q: What made Binita's suggestion about a counsellor gentle?
qa.a: Binita waited, spoke softly, and offered to sit alongside while Darshan booked it, making the step shared rather than a push.

qa.q: What might those evenings have meant to Darshan?
qa.a: For Darshan, quiet company and small help like the laundry probably felt like care without pressure, which is why a simple thanks sounded so big.

grounding: Shows a friend responding to someone withdrawing after failure with company and small help, then gently encouraging counselling.
